templates.name: Principle plus case leads to consequence (S10 trade-off folded in)
Rule or timeline plus observation rejects a premise
Undercut leads to a hedged conclusion
X but not Y, so Z
Two cases or two accounts lead to a conditional or a common ground
Behaviour, design or content reveals a motive or belief (S12 example folded in)
Received view plus counterevidence leads to revision

items.subtype: T3 consequence: two measures applied to the route by which newcomers had gained power
items.passage: In medieval Venice, a contract known as the colleganza enabled merchants with little capital of their own to undertake trading voyages financed by investors who remained at home, the two parties dividing any profits. Economists Diego Puga and Daniel Trefler argue that such contracts enriched a broad group of newcomers, who then used their wealth to press for a larger share of political authority. After 1297, however, a group of exceptionally wealthy merchants made membership in Venice’s parliament hereditary and erected barriers to participation in the most lucrative branches of long-distance commerce. Taken together, these measures most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: barred newly rich merchants from parliament but left them free to compete with established families for the profits of long-distance trade.
made established families more dependent on newcomers, whose investments through the colleganza were needed to finance the most profitable voyages.
blocked outsiders’ path to political power directly while also cutting off the trade wealth that had fueled earlier challenges.
reduced the overall volume of Venice’s long-distance trade by discouraging investors from financing voyages abroad.
items.explanation: New merchants had gained political power by first growing rich through long-distance trade. Making parliament hereditary shut them out of power directly, and the barriers to the most lucrative trade cut off the wealth that had made their earlier rise possible, as C says.

A.why_wrong: Hereditary membership did bar newcomers from parliament, but the text says the same merchants also erected barriers to the most lucrative trade, so newcomers were not left free to compete for its profits.

B.why_wrong: The measures were meant to shut newcomers out; nothing suggests the established families came to depend on them, and the text never says the elite needed newcomers' money.

D.why_wrong: The text says who could take part in the most lucrative trade, not that the total amount of trade fell or that investors stopped financing voyages.

sources.what: Puga and Trefler: long-distance trade enriched a broad group of merchants who pushed for constraints on the executive; colleganza mobilized capital for risky long-distance trade; after 1297 a small group of wealthy merchants made parliamentary participation hereditary and erected barriers to participation in the most lucrative aspects of long-distance trade

items.notes: Area: history (economic history). Steps: (1) newcomers rose by turning trade wealth into political power; (2) the two measures close the political door and the economic route that fed it. Kept premises: A keeps the political half, B keeps the colleganza, D keeps the trade barriers.

fixes: removed 'small' before 'group of exceptionally wealthy merchants' (the NBER abstract says 'a group of extraordinarily rich merchants')

band7.why: Two linked steps (trade wealth fed the newcomers' push for power; the measures close the political door and the wealth route) and all three distractors keep a true piece, but options average about 18 words (gate 20), only one REV or MIX, and the premise sits one sentence back: a strong band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: proposed inheritance rule applied to the offspring of tuskless females
items.passage: During Mozambique’s civil war (1977–1992), ivory poaching eliminated most of the elephants in Gorongosa National Park, and the proportion of females lacking tusks increased from about 18.5 percent to about 51 percent. Evolutionary biologist Shane Campbell-Staton and colleagues documented no tuskless males in the park and proposed that tusklessness results from a dominant mutation on the X chromosome that is lethal to males before birth. Males inherit their single X chromosome from their mothers, whereas females inherit one X chromosome from each parent. If the researchers’ proposal is correct, tuskless females would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: give birth to noticeably fewer male calves than female calves.
pass tusklessness to every daughter, since each daughter inherits an X chromosome from her mother.
have inherited the mutation from their fathers, who carried it without being harmed by it.
disappear from the park within a few generations, since every male that inherits the mutation dies.
items.explanation: Because the mutation kills males, no father can carry it, so a tuskless female has it on only one of her two X chromosomes. About half of her sons would inherit that X and die before birth, while her daughters would survive whether or not they inherit it, so she would bear fewer sons than daughters, as A says.

B.why_wrong: A tuskless female has the mutation on only one of her two X chromosomes, so each daughter has about an even chance of inheriting it, not a certainty.

C.why_wrong: A male that inherited the mutation would die before birth, so no living father could carry it; tuskless females must have inherited it from their mothers.

D.why_wrong: Males with the mutation die, but tuskless females survive and pass it to about half their daughters, so nothing in the proposal implies that tuskless females would vanish within a few generations.

sources.what: Princeton release on Campbell-Staton et al., Science 2021: Mozambican Civil War 1977 to 1992; tuskless females rose from 18.5% to 50.9%; zero tuskless males recorded; trait consistent with X-linked inheritance lethal to males; tuskless mothers' offspring 65.7% female

items.notes: Area: natural science (evolution, genetics). Steps: (1) a male-lethal mutation cannot come from a father, so tuskless females carry one copy; (2) half their sons inherit it and die, skewing births toward daughters (the source reports 65.7% female offspring, left out so the item asks for it). The mechanism is stated as the team's proposal, as the source does.

band7.why: B and C need the full chain (no carrier fathers, so tuskless mothers carry one copy), but the key itself follows from male lethality before birth in about one step; options about 13 words: band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a critic's claim about one translator applied to readers of two authors
items.passage: For decades, many English-speaking readers knew the great nineteenth-century Russian novelists chiefly through the work of one translator, Constance Garnett, who worked fast and produced 71 volumes of Russian literature, among them novels by both Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoevsky. Translation scholar Rachel May has argued that Garnett’s versions homogenized the styles of the authors she translated, smoothing away the idiosyncrasies of narrative voice and dialogue that distinguish one writer’s prose from another’s. If May is right, then readers who knew both of these novelists only through Garnett’s translations would likely have ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: regarded the two novelists’ plots and characters as largely interchangeable with each other.
noticed the sameness of style and attributed it to Garnett rather than to the novelists themselves.
found Garnett’s versions of Dostoevsky more faithful to the originals than her versions of Tolstoy.
perceived the two novelists’ prose as more alike than it is in Russian.
items.explanation: May argues that Garnett gave the authors she translated one smoothed style, erasing what distinguished their voices and dialogue. Readers who met both Tolstoy and Dostoevsky only in her versions were therefore reading one style twice and would likely have found the two writers’ prose more similar than it really is, as D says.

A.why_wrong: May’s claim concerns style, the voice and dialogue of the prose; it gives no reason to think readers would confuse the novelists’ plots and characters.

B.why_wrong: Readers who knew the novels only in Garnett’s English had nothing to compare her versions with, so the text gives no basis for thinking they would trace the sameness to her.

C.why_wrong: The text never compares how faithful Garnett was to one author rather than the other; May’s claim applies to the authors she translated generally.

sources.what: Constance Garnett translated 71 volumes of Russian literature and worked quickly; Rachel May criticized her stylistic homogenizing, erasing idiosyncrasies of narrative voice and dialogue that different authors possessed; Brodsky: English readers can barely tell Tolstoy from Dostoevsky because they are reading Garnett

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature, translation). Steps: (1) one translator, one homogenized style; (2) both novelists read only through her, so their styles seem alike. Kept premises: A stretches style to plot, B keeps the sameness, C keeps the two authors. Brodsky's remark left out so the key is inferred, not quoted.

band7.why: Two steps (one translator, one smoothed style; both authors read only through her); A and B partly right, key paraphrased; options about 15 words and one REV: band 6.

items.subtype: T2 purpose of a design feature, given a stated principle about norms
items.passage: Telling people how their behavior compares with the norm can backfire: such comparative information may draw those whose conduct is better than average back toward the average. Investigating one potential remedy, psychologist P. Wesley Schultz and colleagues gave households in San Marcos, California, written feedback comparing each home’s recent electricity consumption with the neighborhood average; some feedback sheets also carried an emoticon, a frowning face if the household had consumed more energy than average and a smiling face if it had consumed less. For households with below-average consumption, the smiling face was most likely intended to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: shame them into cutting their energy use still further below the average for their neighborhood.
counter the pull of the average by signaling approval of their already low energy use.
show them how far below the neighborhood average their energy use had fallen.
encourage households that used more energy than average to imitate their thriftier neighbors.
items.explanation: The text says a comparison with the norm can draw households that are doing better than average back toward it, so low-use households told the average risk using more. A smile signals approval, so it tells those households that their low use is good, which works against that pull, as B says.

A.why_wrong: A smile signals approval, not shame; it was attached for households already below the average, to keep their use low rather than to push it lower.

C.why_wrong: The comparison with the neighborhood average already showed each household where it stood; the face was added to that comparison, so its purpose was something else.

D.why_wrong: High-use households received a frown on their own sheets; a smile on a low-use household’s sheet was meant for that household.

sources.what: Schultz 2007 (ScienceDaily): households in San Marcos got their actual energy use and how it compared with the average; frugal households given only the data used more; an emoticon was attached, a smiley face for below-average and a frown for above-average households; praised frugal households did not increase use

items.notes: Area: social science (psychology). Steps: (1) the norm pulls low users up toward the average; (2) a smile signals approval and so counters that pull. Kept premises: A keeps conservation, C keeps the comparison, D keeps the frown condition. The result (smile households did not increase) left out so the item asks for the purpose.

band7.why: Needed premise is sentence 1, two sentences from the blank, and C is true-but-not-the-step, but A (shame) and D (wrong group) each fall to one fact; options about 15 words: band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a finding about what predicts word length applied to two equally frequent words
items.passage: In the 1930s, linguist George Kingsley Zipf observed that frequently used words tend to be short, and for decades word length was attributed principally to frequency of use. Analyzing texts in numerous languages, cognitive scientists Steven Piantadosi, Harry Tily, and Edward Gibson found that a word’s length is better predicted by its average information content, which is low when the surrounding context typically makes the word easy to anticipate, than by its frequency. If two words in a language occurred equally often but one usually appeared in contexts where it was highly predictable, that word would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: be about as long as the other word, since the two words are used equally often.
be longer than the other word, which would help listeners tell the two apart.
be the shorter of the two, since it typically carries less information where it occurs.
gradually be replaced by a less predictable word that conveys more information.
items.explanation: A word that is easy to guess from its context has low information content, and Piantadosi’s team found that low information content goes with short words. Since frequency is the same for both words, the easily predicted one should be the shorter, as C says.

A.recipe: older view in place of the finding (MIX)
A.why_wrong: Equal frequency would predict equal length only on the older frequency explanation; the team found information content a better predictor, and the two words differ in that.

B.why_wrong: Low information content goes with shorter words, not longer ones, and the text says nothing about length helping listeners tell words apart.

D.why_wrong: The text is about which words are short, not about words being replaced over time.

sources.what: Piantadosi, Tily and Gibson, PNAS 2011: across languages, average information content is a much better predictor of word length than frequency, challenging Zipf's frequency account

items.notes: Area: social science (linguistics). Steps: (1) easy to predict means low information content; (2) low information content means a shorter word, with frequency held equal so Zipf's account cannot decide. Kept premises: A keeps frequency (the old view), B keeps length, D keeps information content.

band7.why: Key needs the aside defining information content plus the finding; A is a strong partly-right (the old frequency view), B and D fall quickly; options about 15 words: band 6.

items.subtype: T6 function of a behavior, from a perception experiment
items.passage: As a large animal approaches, a rattlesnake shakes its rattle progressively faster until, at a certain point, it abruptly switches to a considerably higher rate of roughly 60 to 100 shakes per second. To investigate how human listeners perceive this escalating display, neurobiologist Boris Chagnaud and his colleagues moved participants through a virtual grassland toward a concealed snake whose rattling followed the same pattern; when the rate suddenly jumped, participants judged the snake to be nearer than it actually was. This observation suggests that the abrupt switch most likely serves to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: make an approaching animal stop farther from the snake than it otherwise would.
convince an approaching animal that the snake is larger than it actually is.
signal that the snake is about to strike, regardless of how far away the intruder is.
make the rattle audible to animals that are still too far away to hear the slower rattling.
items.explanation: When the rate jumped, listeners believed the snake was closer than it really was. An animal that thinks it is already near the snake would halt sooner, leaving more distance between them, so the switch likely serves to keep intruders farther away, as A says.

B.why_wrong: Participants misjudged how far away the snake was, not how big it was.

C.why_wrong: The switch comes as the intruder gets close and changes how near the snake seems; the text gives no sign that it announces a strike, let alone at any distance.

D.why_wrong: The high rate begins only after the intruder has come close; animals still far away hear the slower rattling, so the switch is not aimed at them.

sources.what: Forsthofer, Chagnaud et al., Current Biology 2021: rattling rate increases as threats approach, then abruptly switches to 60 to 100 Hz; in a virtual reality grassland the sudden increase made participants underestimate their distance to the snake, creating a distance safety margin

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior, perception). Steps: (1) the jump makes the snake seem closer; (2) an intruder who thinks it is close stops sooner, keeping a margin. Note: an official Command of Evidence item studies rattlesnake stress with a companion; this subject (rattle frequency and distance perception) is different.

fixes: researchers trimmed to 'neurobiologist Boris Chagnaud and his colleagues' (the cited page names only Chagnaud)

band7.why: Two steps (judged nearer, so the intruder halts sooner); B and D keep true pieces, key paraphrased away from the passage; options about 15 words: band 6.

items.subtype: T2 motive inferred from the timing of an author's decision
items.passage: Like most of Charles Dickens’s novels, Martin Chuzzlewit was published in monthly installments, appearing between 1843 and 1844, and Dickens was still writing the novel while its installments were going on sale. Sales of the early installments were noticeably lower than those of his previous novels. Then, at the end of the fifth installment, the novel’s young protagonist abruptly announces that he will go to the United States, and later installments follow him there through a lengthy succession of unfamiliar American settings and characters. The timing of this development suggests that Dickens ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: had planned from the start to move the story to the United States after its fifth installment.
had run out of ideas for the novel’s English scenes, since he was still writing the novel while its installments were going on sale.
was responding to requests from readers of his earlier novels for stories set outside England.
took advantage of serial publication to try to attract more buyers to a slow-selling novel.
items.explanation: Because Dickens was still writing the novel as its installments went on sale, he could change course after seeing how the first parts sold. The abrupt move to America came after sales of the early installments fell short of his earlier novels, so it was likely an attempt to draw more buyers, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The change is described as abrupt and came after weak early sales, while Dickens was still writing the novel, which points to a decision made along the way, not a plan from the start.

B.why_wrong: Dickens was indeed writing as the installments appeared, but that was true from the start; what the change followed was weak sales, and the text never suggests he had run short of ideas.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions only the low sales of this novel’s early installments; it never mentions any requests from readers of his earlier novels.

sources.what: Martin Chuzzlewit: serialized 1843 to 1844; early sales of the monthly parts were lower than those of previous works, so Dickens changed the plot to send the title character to the United States

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature, publishing history). Steps: (1) writing month by month let him change course; (2) the change followed weak sales, so it aimed to lift them. Sales figures left out (only one secondary page gives 20,000). His 1842 American tour not mentioned and no option uses it, so no second motive is defensible. Reviewer: the source (Slater note on the cited page) puts Martin's sudden announcement at the end of Part V, so the passage now says the fifth installment; the writing-schedule clause is cut back to what the page implies (he changed the plot after weak early sales); B, a plain off-topic claim, is now a rival cause that keeps the schedule premise.

fixes: 'in the sixth installment' changed to 'at the end of the fifth installment', where the cited page's Slater note puts Martin's sudden announcement

'wrote each installment only shortly before it went on sale' softened to 'was still writing the novel while its installments were going on sale' (implied by the page: he changed the plot after weak early sales)
B (plain off-topic) replaced by a partly-right rival cause that keeps the writing-schedule premise; A reworded to the fifth installment

band7.why: Two steps (still writing, so able to change course; change followed weak sales); after the fix A and B keep true premises, but C is a plain rival motive and options average about 17 words: band 6.

items.subtype: Timeline rejects a premise: the horse lineage spread a thousand years after the expansion
items.passage: Around 3000 BCE, herders of the Yamnaya culture expanded from the steppes north of the Black Sea into much of Europe, a migration that many archaeologists have attributed to horseback riding and linked to the dispersal of Indo-European languages. Analyzing the genomes of 273 ancient horses, Pablo Librado, Ludovic Orlando, and colleagues traced all modern domestic horses to a lineage from the steppe’s lower Volga-Don region; apart from two individuals found on the steppe, no sampled horse older than about 2200 BCE belonged to it, and the lineage replaced most other horse populations across Eurasia only from about 2000 BCE, together with chariots. The team therefore concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: Yamnaya herders brought into Europe the horses that later replaced Eurasia’s other horse populations.
the Yamnaya expansion into Europe probably did not rely on horses of the lineage that spread later.
Indo-European languages could not have reached Europe before domestic horses spread there around 2000 BCE.
chariots were developed in Europe and later carried east to the lower Volga-Don region.
items.explanation: The Yamnaya reached Europe around 3000 BCE, but apart from two steppe horses, no sampled horse older than about 2200 BCE belonged to the lineage of modern domestic horses, which spread across Eurasia only from about 2000 BCE. Horses of that lineage therefore could not have carried the expansion into Europe a thousand years earlier, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The lineage is absent from sampled horses older than about 2200 BCE apart from two on the steppe, and it spread across Eurasia only from about 2000 BCE, about a thousand years after the Yamnaya reached Europe, so the herders could not have brought those horses with them.

C.why_wrong: The finding separates the expansion from this horse lineage; it does not move the expansion itself, which the text dates to around 3000 BCE, and says nothing about when languages arrived.

D.why_wrong: The text places the lineage’s origin in the lower Volga-Don region and says it spread outward with chariots, not that chariots came from Europe.

sources.what: Librado et al., Nature 2021: 273 ancient horse genomes; modern domestic horses (DOM2) originated in the lower Volga-Don region and replaced most other populations from about 2000 BC, together with spoke-wheeled chariots; this rejects the association between horseback riding and the Yamnaya expansion into Europe around 3000 BC; genetic continuity with DOM2 rejected for horses older than about 2200 BC, except two late Yamnaya horses from Turganik east of the lower Volga-Don

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology (ancient DNA). Steps: (1) compare dates: expansion about 3000 BCE, horse lineage spreads about 2000 BCE; (2) so the lineage cannot have carried the expansion. Kept premises: A keeps the replacement, C keeps the languages and 2000 BCE, D keeps chariots and the Volga-Don.

band7.why: Negative key, three dates with an exception the key must honour, and every distractor keeps a true piece (A rescues the received view, D reverses the direction), but one date comparison settles it and options average about 15 words: a strong band 6.

items.subtype: X but not Y: tariffed and untariffed goods rose alike, so a washer-only estimate of the cost falls short
items.passage: In 2012, the United States imposed antidumping duties on washing machines from South Korea and Mexico, and in 2016 on those from China, yet washer prices barely changed, partly because manufacturers relocated production to other countries. In 2018, by contrast, tariffs covered washers from virtually all exporting countries. Economists Aaron Flaaen, Ali Hortaçsu, and Felix Tintelnot found that washer prices subsequently rose by nearly 12 percent and that the prices of clothes dryers, which were not taxed but are often bought along with washers, increased by about the same amount. These findings suggest that an estimate of the tariffs’ cost to US consumers calculated only from washer prices would ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: be accurate, since the tariffs applied only to washers and not to dryers.
understate that cost, since manufacturers again moved production to countries that the tariffs did not cover.
understate that cost, since consumers also paid more for a product that the tariffs did not cover.
overstate that cost, since washer prices had barely changed after the earlier duties on particular countries.
items.explanation: Dryers were not taxed, yet their prices rose about as much as washer prices did, and the two are often bought together, so the tariffs raised what consumers paid for dryers as well. An estimate calculated only from washer prices would leave that extra cost out and so would come in too low, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The tariffs did cover only washers, but dryer prices rose by about as much as washer prices; an estimate that ignored dryers would miss that increase, so it would not be accurate.

B.why_wrong: Moving production abroad is what happened after the earlier duties; the 2018 tariffs covered washers from virtually all exporting countries and washer prices rose, and a move abroad would not make a washer-only estimate too low in any case.

D.why_wrong: What happened after the earlier duties says nothing about the size of the 2018 cost, and the rise in dryer prices means a washer-only estimate would leave costs out, not count too much.

sources.what: Flaaen, Hortacsu and Tintelnot, AER 2020, abstract: 2012 and 2016 antidumping duties on South Korea and China were accompanied by minor price movements and production relocation; 2018 tariffs on nearly all source countries raised washer prices nearly 12 percent; dryer prices, not subject to tariffs, rose by an equivalent amount; factoring in dryer prices, the tariffs imply a tariff elasticity of consumer prices above one (so a washer-only figure falls short). Washers and dryers bought together: general knowledge, a smaller detail.

items.notes: Area: social science (economics). S6: washers taxed, dryers not, prices rose alike. Reviewer hardened it (the old key was close to a summary of the two stated facts): the lead-in now asks what a washer-only estimate of the cost would do. Steps: (1) the untaxed dryer rose with the taxed washer and the two are bought together, so the tariffs raised dryer prices too; (2) an estimate from washer prices leaves that out and comes in low. B and C share the phrase 'not cover' with different referents (countries, a product); A keeps the tariff's scope; D keeps the earlier episode. No option says washer prices rose less than the tariff, which the passage cannot rule out. The source's own estimate accounts for dryer prices.

fixes: hardened: lead-in now asks what a washer-only estimate of the 2018 cost would do, so the key needs two linked steps and is no longer a summary
options rebuilt as a near-miss set: B and C share 'not cover' with different referents, A keeps the tariff scope, D the earlier episode; old A (shared parts) and old B dropped
added that dryers are often bought together with washers so the dryer rise reads as a tariff effect
review.safety_fix: safety solve noted the 2012 duties covered South Korea and Mexico, not South Korea and China; passage and option D corrected (2016 duties covered China)

band7.why: After hardening the key needs two linked steps (dryer rise is a tariff cost; a washer-only estimate omits it) and all three distractors are partly right (2 MIX), but the dryer premise is the sentence before the blank and options average about 16 words: a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Received view plus counterevidence leads to a revised account of the within-country link
items.passage: Within any single country, individuals with higher incomes tend to report greater life satisfaction than those with lower incomes. In the 1970s, however, economist Richard Easterlin reported that wealthier countries were not reliably happier on average than poorer ones, a pattern frequently interpreted to mean that people judge their incomes primarily against those of the people around them. Reassessing the question with decades of survey data from many countries, economists Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers found that average life satisfaction rises with national income at about the same rate at which individual satisfaction rises with individual income within a country. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the link between income and life satisfaction within a country probably does not come mainly from comparisons with other people’s incomes.
people’s life satisfaction is not affected at all by how their incomes compare with those of other people.
residents of wealthier countries are more satisfied than residents of poorer countries chiefly because they compare themselves with people in poorer countries.
a person’s life satisfaction depends more on the average income of his or her country than on his or her own income.
items.explanation: If people judged their incomes only against those around them, a rise in a whole country’s income would leave everyone’s relative position unchanged, so richer countries would be no happier. Stevenson and Wolfers found instead that average satisfaction rises with national income about as fast as individual satisfaction rises with individual income. That suggests that the amount people earn, not mainly how it ranks, explains why richer people within a country are more satisfied, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The findings weaken the view that comparisons are the main reason income matters, but rates that are only about the same cannot show that comparisons play no part at all.

C.why_wrong: The text gives no evidence that people compare themselves with residents of other countries; the findings point to income itself, not to a different kind of comparison.

D.why_wrong: The findings say national income and individual income go with satisfaction at about the same rate, not that a country’s average income matters more than a person’s own.

sources.what: Stevenson and Wolfers, NBER w14282 (2008), Reassessing the Easterlin Paradox: clear positive link between average subjective well-being and GDP per capita; the cross-country relationship resembles the within-country income and happiness relationship; a clear role for absolute income and a more limited role for relative income comparisons

items.notes: Area: social science (economics, psychology). Reviewer hardened it: the doubt frame ('calling into question the assumption that') let three stated or supported claims fall at once, so the frame is now positive. Steps: (1) a comparison account predicts no rise in average satisfaction when a whole country grows richer, since no one's rank changes; (2) the national rise matches the individual one, so the within-country link of sentence 1 is not mainly about comparison. Key hedged to the source ('a more limited role for relative income comparisons'). B overstates the key, C rescues the comparison view with another reference group, D misreads 'about the same rate'. No option mentions a satiation point, which the passage does not address.

fixes: hardened: doubt frame replaced by a positive frame; key is now a hedged revision of the within-country link (source: 'a more limited role for relative income comparisons')
distractors rebuilt as partly right: overreach of the key (no effect), rescue of the comparison view (other countries), wrong level (country income over own income)
plain words: 'evaluate their incomes' to 'judge their incomes' (other long words kept for the tier's register gate)

band7.why: After hardening: negative hedged key, premise two sentences back, three partly-right distractors (EXT, REV rescue, MIX), options about 20 words; it meets several band-7 signals, but the chain is the one the passage sets up step by step, so judged a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Opposite individual outcomes lead to a 'depends on' conclusion
items.passage: Whole-grain sourdough bread is widely presumed to be nutritionally superior to industrially produced white bread. In a randomized trial led by Tal Korem, Eran Elinav, and Eran Segal, a group of healthy adults ate each type of bread for a week, one after the other. Averaged across participants, the two breads produced no significantly different effects on blood sugar or other clinical indicators; individual responses, however, varied considerably, and which bread produced the smaller rise in blood sugar for a given person could be predicted from measurements of that person’s gut bacteria taken before the trial. These results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: sourdough bread lowers blood sugar in most people, although the effect is too small to detect in an average.
the effect of sourdough on a person’s blood sugar may depend partly on that person’s gut bacteria.
the kind of bread a person eats has little effect on that person’s blood sugar.
eating a single kind of bread for a week can change which bacteria live in a person’s gut.
items.explanation: On average the breads did not differ, yet for each person one bread produced a lower rise in blood sugar, and which one could be predicted from the person’s gut bacteria. So whether sourdough helps depends on the person, and the bacteria appear to be part of what decides it, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says responses varied and that the lower-response bread differed from person to person, so sourdough did not produce the lower response in most people.

C.why_wrong: The breads matched only on average; individuals responded differently to them, so bread type did affect individual blood sugar.

D.why_wrong: The bacteria were measured before the trial to predict responses; the text does not report any change in them caused by the bread.

sources.what: Korem et al., Cell Metabolism 2017: randomized crossover, one week each of industrial white bread and whole-grain sourdough; no significant differential effects of bread type on clinical parameters; glycemic responses varied between people; the bread inducing the lower response could be predicted from microbiome data before the intervention

items.notes: Area: natural science (nutrition, microbiology). Steps: (1) no average difference but opposite individual responses means the effect is person-specific; (2) prediction from gut bacteria ties it to a personal trait. Participant count dropped (not on the cited page).

fixes: dropped '20' participants (not on the cited page); 'consumed' to 'ate'

band7.why: Two steps (no average difference but opposite individual responses; prediction from gut bacteria) and A, C, D each keep a true piece, but options average about 17 words and only one REV: band 6.

items.subtype: Received view (stylistic change) plus new evidence (air pollution)
items.passage: Over their careers, the British painter Joseph Mallord William Turner and the French painter Claude Monet both moved from crisp, sharply outlined scenes toward hazy, pale compositions in which contours dissolve. This transition has usually been interpreted as an evolution in artistic style. Climate scientists Anna Lea Albright and Peter Huybers, however, measured contrast and color in nearly 100 of the two artists’ paintings and found that the works grew hazier as emissions of sulfur dioxide, a pollutant that forms tiny light-scattering particles in the atmosphere, increased in the cities where they painted. This finding suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: Turner and Monet deliberately chose pale colors in order to protest the spread of industrial pollution.
audiences admired the artists’ later, hazier paintings less than their earlier, crisper ones.
paintings made in cities with clean air show sharper outlines than any painting by Turner or Monet.
the hazier look of the artists’ later works may partly record changes in the air they observed.
items.explanation: The paintings grew hazier as a pollutant that scatters light increased in the air where the artists worked. That suggests the haze in the later works may reflect real changes in the atmosphere they were painting, not only a change in style, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The study links haze in the paintings to pollution levels; the text says nothing about the artists intending a protest.

B.why_wrong: The text never discusses how audiences received the earlier or later paintings.

C.why_wrong: The study measured only Turner’s and Monet’s paintings; it made no comparison with paintings from cities with clean air.

sources.what: Albright and Huybers, PNAS: 60 Turner and 38 Monet paintings; local sulfur dioxide emissions strongly predict changes in contrast and whiteness; the shift toward hazier contours and whiter palettes is consistent with the optical effects of higher aerosol concentrations

items.notes: Area: humanities (art history) with atmospheric science. Paper year (2023) left out of the passage, since official passages run to 2022. Hedged key ('may partly'), as the authors call paintings an imperfect proxy.

items.subtype: Received view (honeybees can replace wild pollinators) plus counterevidence
items.passage: As populations of wild bees and other pollinating insects have declined across many agricultural regions, it has often been assumed that farmers can compensate for the loss by bringing in hives of managed honeybees. Ecologist Lucas Garibaldi and colleagues examined flower visitation and fruit production in 41 crop systems worldwide. Visits by wild insects increased the proportion of flowers that set fruit in every system, whereas honeybee visits did so in only 14 percent of them, and the benefit from wild insects persisted even where honeybees were abundant. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: managed honeybees may not fully replace wild insects as pollinators of crops.
honeybees reduce fruit production in most crops by crowding wild insects away from flowers.
crops visited often by honeybees produce as much fruit without wild insects as with them.
farmers should stop bringing honeybee hives to their fields and rely on wild insects instead.
items.explanation: Wild insects raised fruit set in every crop system, honeybees in only a few, and the wild insects helped even where honeybees were plentiful. Adding honeybees therefore does not seem to make up for losing wild insects, as A says.

B.why_wrong: Honeybee visits failed to increase fruit set in most systems, but the text never says they reduced it or drove wild insects away.

C.why_wrong: Wild insects raised fruit set even where honeybees were abundant, so these crops did produce more fruit with wild insects.

D.why_wrong: The findings show that wild insects add something honeybees do not; they do not show that honeybees are useless or that hives should be removed.

sources.what: Garibaldi et al., Science 2013: 41 crop systems worldwide; fruit set increased with wild insect visitation in all systems but with honey bee visitation in only 14%; wild insects enhanced fruit set regardless of honey bee abundance

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology, agriculture). Received view stated as an assumption, then the comparison across 41 systems. Distractors: EXT, REV, REC.

items.subtype: Mechanism plus experiment applied to a new case (glass buildings)
items.passage: Bats navigate in darkness by echolocation, emitting calls and listening for echoes from surfaces ahead. A smooth vertical surface, however, reflects a bat’s calls away from the animal when the bat approaches at an angle, so that no echo returns until the bat is extremely close. In a flight room, behavioral ecologist Stefan Greif and colleagues observed bats flying toward a smooth vertical plate; the bats avoided it in only about a third of their approaches and otherwise collided with it, apparently perceiving it as unobstructed space. This finding suggests that buildings with extensive glass facades ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: are easier for bats to detect than cliffs, trees, and other rough natural surfaces.
attract bats because smooth glass returns their calls more strongly than rough walls do.
may be dangerous to bats, which could mistake the glass for a clear flight path.
endanger bats only on nights when no lights are on inside the buildings.
items.explanation: A smooth vertical surface sends a bat’s calls away, so it seems like open space until the bat is very close, and bats in the experiment usually flew into such a plate. Large panes of glass are smooth and vertical, so they could fool bats in the same way, as C says.

A.why_wrong: Smooth surfaces send calls away instead of back, so they are harder, not easier, for bats to detect.

B.why_wrong: The text says a smooth surface reflects calls away from the bat, so it returns weaker echoes, not stronger ones.

D.why_wrong: The bats were misled by sound, not sight; the text gives no reason to think lighting inside a building would make glass safe.

sources.what: Max Planck Society release on Greif, Zsebok et al., Science 2017: smooth vertical surfaces reflect echolocation calls away and are perceived as open flyways; in only one third of observed approaches did the bats avoid colliding with the plate; frequent collisions with glass facades of buildings

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior, conservation). Principle (acoustic mirror) plus case (glass walls). Species left unnamed.

fixes: source swapped to the Max Planck release, which states the one-third figure and glass facades

items.subtype: Rival explanation undercuts the evidence: the holes are not conclusive
items.passage: In 1995, archaeologist Ivan Turk excavated a fragment of a juvenile cave bear’s thighbone perforated by two round holes from Divje Babe, a cave in Slovenia whose deposits also contain stone tools manufactured by Neanderthals. Turk and his colleagues have argued that the bone is a flute made by Neanderthals. Archaeologist Francesco d’Errico, however, identified similar holes in another juvenile cave bear’s thighbone from the same cave, and paleontologist Cajus Diedrich has attributed such perforations to scavenging cave hyenas. Considered together, these observations indicate that the holes in Turk’s bone ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: were most likely made by cave hyenas rather than by Neanderthals.
do not by themselves show that Neanderthals made the bone into an instrument.
were probably made after the Neanderthals who used the cave had left it.
show that Neanderthals also made flutes from the bones of other animals.
items.explanation: Turk reads the holes as the work of Neanderthals, but similar holes occur in another cave bear bone from the same cave, and they can be explained as the bites of hyenas. With a second explanation available, the holes alone cannot settle whether the bone is a flute, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The hyena account is offered as a possible explanation; the text gives no evidence that rules out Turk’s view, so it cannot show which is more likely.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about when the holes were made relative to the Neanderthals’ use of the cave.

D.why_wrong: The text discusses only cave bear bones and does not establish that this bone is a flute at all.

sources.what: Divje Babe flute: juvenile cave bear femur found in 1995 in excavations led by Ivan Turk, with two complete holes on one side; Turk argues for a Neanderthal instrument; d'Errico (1998) noted similar holes on a young cave bear femur from the same site; Diedrich (2015) attributed the holes to spotted hyena scavenging

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology (Paleolithic). S5: claim plus rival explanation, hedged key. Frame varied from 2.18 ('Considered together, these observations indicate').

items.subtype: Rival explanation undercuts an interpretation: the structures may not be original tissue
items.passage: In 2005, paleontologist Mary Schweitzer and colleagues dissolved the mineral from a fossil Tyrannosaurus rex bone and recovered flexible, branching tubes and tiny round bodies that resembled blood vessels and cells, suggesting that some original soft tissue had survived for about 68 million years. Thomas Kaye and colleagues later showed that films of bacteria coating the hollow spaces inside a bone can, once the bone itself is dissolved, leave structures closely resembling vessels and cells, and they found such films in bones of many dinosaur and mammal species. Kaye’s findings suggest that the structures Schweitzer recovered ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: were formed by bacteria living inside the dinosaur’s bones while the animal was still alive.
prove that original soft tissue cannot survive in a fossil for millions of years.
are common in mammal bones but rarely occur in the bones of dinosaurs.
may not be remains of the dinosaur’s own tissue, as Schweitzer’s team had thought.
items.explanation: Kaye’s team showed that bacterial films inside bone can leave casts that look like vessels and cells, and that such films are widespread in fossil bones. The structures from the T. rex bone could therefore be such casts, so they may not be the dinosaur’s own tissue, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The films coat the hollow spaces in bone; nothing in the text says the bacteria lived there while the dinosaur was alive.

B.why_wrong: Kaye’s findings offer another explanation for these structures; they do not show that soft tissue can never survive.

C.why_wrong: Kaye’s team found such films in bones of many dinosaur species as well as mammals.

sources.what: Kaye, Gaugler and Sawlowicz, PLoS ONE 2008, Dinosaurian soft tissues interpreted as bacterial biofilms: structures earlier treated as preserved soft tissue (Schweitzer et al. 2005) mimic vessels and osteocytes; biofilms form endocasts that, once dissolved out of the bone, mimic real blood vessels and osteocytes; similar coatings found across many dinosaur and mammal genera

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleontology). Hedged key. Kaye's carbon dating of the film left out so D needs the inference. Topic (T. rex soft tissue, 2005) had press attention; the 2008 biofilm reading is the less familiar half.

items.subtype: Rule (island isolated for five million years) plus dated tools rejects a land route
items.passage: The Greek island of Crete has been separated from the mainland and every other landmass by open sea for more than five million years. During archaeological surveys near the village of Plakias, on the island’s southwestern coast, Thomas Strasser and colleagues discovered hand axes and other stone implements of a type manufactured by early humans, in geological deposits indicating that some of the tools are at least 130,000 years old. Previously, the earliest documented sea voyages in the Mediterranean were thought to have occurred more than 100,000 years later. The team therefore concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: people were crossing open water in some kind of vessel far earlier than had been thought.
Crete was still connected to the mainland by land about 130,000 years ago.
the tools were carried to Crete by much later settlers who had collected them on the mainland.
early humans lived on Crete without interruption from 130,000 years ago to the present.
items.explanation: Crete has been cut off by sea for more than five million years, yet early humans left tools there at least 130,000 years ago. They must have crossed open water to reach the island, which pushes sea travel far back before the earliest voyages previously known, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The text says Crete has been separated from every landmass by sea for more than five million years.

C.why_wrong: The tools lie in geological deposits that date them to at least 130,000 years ago, so they were not brought later.

D.why_wrong: The tools show that people reached Crete long ago, not that they lived there continuously ever since.

sources.what: Strasser et al., Hesperia 79 (2010), abstract: Plakias region of southwestern Crete; Lower Palaeolithic occupation dated by geological context to at least 130,000 years ago; separation of more than 5,000,000 years from any landmass implies seacraft; pushes Mediterranean seafaring back by more than 100,000 years

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. Rule plus observation: isolated island plus old tools means sea crossing. 'Some of the tools' because the 130,000-year date applies to some sites only.

fixes: source swapped to the Hesperia abstract, which states the 130,000-year minimum, more than 5,000,000 years of isolation and the 100,000-year push-back

items.subtype: Time sequence leads to an onset bound ('by the twelfth century')
items.passage: Walrus ivory was prized in medieval Europe for luxury carvings. Atlantic walruses belong to two genetic lineages, and during the Middle Ages one of these lineages inhabited only waters accessible to people based in Greenland, a remote outpost where Norse settlers had established farms in the late tenth century. Analyzing DNA from walrus skull fragments and tusks recovered at European archaeological sites dating from roughly 900 to 1400, Bastiaan Star, James Barrett, and colleagues determined that the earliest specimens came mostly from the other lineage but that from the twelfth century onward most came from the Greenland lineage. The researchers therefore concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: walruses of the Greenland lineage moved closer to European coasts during the twelfth century.
Greenland’s settlers supplied most of Europe’s walrus ivory from the time they first arrived.
by the twelfth century, Norse Greenland had become Europe’s main source of walrus ivory.
European demand for walrus ivory declined sharply after the twelfth century.
items.explanation: Only people based in Greenland could hunt walruses of the Greenland lineage, and from the twelfth century nearly all the ivory found in Europe came from that lineage. So by then Greenland’s Norse settlers were supplying most of Europe’s walrus ivory, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text says this lineage lived only in waters reached from Greenland; it gives no evidence that the walruses moved toward Europe.

B.why_wrong: The earliest European specimens came mostly from the other lineage, so Greenland was not the main supplier from the start.

D.why_wrong: The text reports where the ivory came from, not how demand for it changed.

sources.what: Star et al., Proc. R. Soc. B 2018: Atlantic walrus has two mitochondrial clades, one exclusively accessible to Greenlanders; origins of 23 European specimens dated 900 to 1400; early trade mostly eastern lineage, from the 12th century onward almost exclusively western (Greenland) lineage

items.notes: Area: history (medieval trade, ancient DNA). S7 onset bound. Arrival of Norse settlers about 985 given only as 'late tenth century'.

fixes: 'nearly all' to 'most' for the later specimens (10 of 12 from the 1120s on, per the paper)

items.subtype: Choice of medium reveals an aim
items.passage: In 1946, the American sculptor and printmaker Elizabeth Catlett went to Mexico City, where she began working at the Taller de Gráfica Popular (People’s Graphic Arts Workshop). The workshop specialized in linoleum cuts, prints produced from carved blocks of linoleum, a technique that is easy to master, produces inexpensive prints, and allows large editions. Its artists often addressed social and political themes in posters and leaflets as well as in individual prints, and many of Catlett’s prints there drew on images that working people in Mexico would readily recognize. Catlett’s embrace of this medium most likely reflected ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: a wish to finish each work quickly enough to sell it on the same day it was made.
her belief that art should reach a wide public rather than only a small group of collectors.
her view that the carved blocks were more valuable as artworks than the prints made from them.
the difficulty of obtaining the stone and wood she needed for sculpture in Mexico City.
items.explanation: Linoleum cuts are cheap and can be printed in large numbers, and Catlett’s prints used images familiar to working people. Choosing such a medium suggests she wanted her art to reach many ordinary viewers, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The technique is described as easy to work with, but the text says nothing about selling prints on the day they were made.

C.why_wrong: The medium’s advantages lie in the prints, which are cheap and numerous; nothing suggests she valued the blocks over the prints.

D.why_wrong: The text never mentions any shortage of sculpture materials.

sources.what: MoMA: the Taller de Grafica Popular specialized in linoleum cut, a technique that is easy to work with, produces inexpensive prints, and can accommodate large editions; Catlett maintained a deep belief in the democratic power of printed art to reach a large audience

items.notes: Area: humanities (visual art). Design reveals purpose. Her arrival in 1946 and the familiar imagery (Notre Dame museum note) are smaller details, not separately checked.

fixes: 'settled in Mexico City and joined' to 'went to Mexico City, where she began working at' (sources split between 1946 and 1947 for settling)

items.subtype: Two populations raised alike still differ, so the difference is inherited
items.passage: Many moths are attracted to artificial lights at night, where they are easily captured by predators. Ecologists Florian Altermatt and Dieter Ebert collected young caterpillars of the small ermine moth from areas subjected to intense light pollution for decades and from areas with naturally dark night skies. They reared all of the caterpillars under identical laboratory conditions and then released the adult moths in a dark room with a single light. Moths from the light-polluted populations were significantly less likely to fly toward the light. This difference suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: moths from dark-sky areas would become less attracted to light after spending a few nights near city lights.
light pollution has reduced the number of moths that live in urban areas.
moths raised in a laboratory are less attracted to light than moths that grow up in the wild.
the urban moths’ weaker attraction to light is likely inherited rather than learned from their own experience.
items.explanation: All the moths grew up under the same conditions, so differences in their own experience of light cannot explain why the urban moths flew to the light less often. The difference most likely comes from their parents and is inherited, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The study did not expose dark-sky moths to city lights; and if experience changed attraction, raising both groups alike would have erased the difference.

B.why_wrong: The study compared behavior, not numbers of moths in urban areas.

C.why_wrong: All the moths tested were raised in the laboratory; the study made no comparison with moths raised in the wild.

sources.what: Altermatt and Ebert, Biology Letters 2016: small ermine moth (Yponomeuta cagnagella) from 10 populations reared from early-instar larvae under standardized conditions; moths from areas with decades of high light pollution showed significantly reduced flight-to-light behaviour

items.notes: Area: natural science (evolution, ecology). S6: same rearing, different behavior, so heritable.

items.subtype: Design reveals purpose
items.passage: Many pedestrians now walk while looking down at their smartphones. In 2016, after a teenager who was looking at her phone was struck and killed by a tram, the German city of Augsburg experimented with a new kind of signal at two tram stops. The crossings there already had ordinary traffic lights mounted on poles. The city installed additional strips of lights in the pavement along the edge of the tracks. These lights flash red whenever it is dangerous to cross. City officials most likely placed the new lights in the pavement because ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: lights in the ground cost less to install than lights on poles.
tram drivers approaching the stops can see lights in the ground more easily than lights on poles.
people looking down at their phones might notice them more easily than lights on poles.
the ordinary traffic lights at the two stops had stopped working.
items.explanation: The text says many people look down at their phones as they walk and that the lights were added after a girl looking at her phone was killed. Lights in the ground are where such people are looking, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about what the lights cost.

B.why_wrong: The lights flash when it is not safe to cross, so they are meant for people on foot, not for tram drivers.

D.why_wrong: The text says the crossings already had traffic lights; it does not say they had stopped working.

sources.what: Augsburg 2016: red LED lights embedded in the pavement at tram crossings after a 15-year-old girl looking at her smartphone was killed by a tram; officials said the normal traffic light is not in the line of sight of many pedestrians

items.notes: Area: social science (urban design, safety). Easy: short sentences, one step.

items.subtype: Rule applied to a case (license ends after 26 loans)
items.passage: Public libraries pay publishers for licenses that allow them to lend electronic books. Each license permits a library to lend one digital copy of a particular book to one reader at a time. In 2011, the publisher HarperCollins announced that its licenses would expire after an e-book had been borrowed 26 times. After that, a library that wanted to continue lending the book would need to purchase another license. Under this new arrangement, a library with an extremely popular HarperCollins e-book would probably ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: have to pay for that e-book again sooner than for one that few people borrow.
be able to lend that e-book to more than 26 readers at the same time without paying more.
stop buying e-books from every publisher other than HarperCollins.
pay less for that e-book than it would pay for a printed copy.
items.explanation: A license ends after 26 checkouts. A popular e-book reaches 26 checkouts quickly, so the library would need to buy a new license for it sooner than for a book few people borrow, as A says.

B.why_wrong: Each license lets the library lend one copy to one reader at a time, not to many readers at once.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about libraries refusing to buy from other publishers.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no prices and never compares e-books with printed copies.

sources.what: HarperCollins 2011 cap: library e-book loans limited to 26 check-outs, after which the library would have to repurchase the e-book

items.notes: Area: humanities and social science (publishing, libraries). Easy S2: rule plus case.

fixes: source swapped to a page that states the repurchase after 26 loans

items.subtype: Two settings with opposite outcomes lead to a 'some places but not others' conclusion
items.passage: Gardeners and farmers usually welcome earthworms in their soil, and for good reason. The worms pull dead leaves and other plant material down into the soil, which loosens the soil and makes it more fertile. But many hardwood forests in the western Great Lakes region contained no earthworms at all until people accidentally introduced them, for example when anglers dumped their leftover fishing bait. In these forests, many wildflowers and young trees take root in a thick, spongy layer of rotting leaves that covers the forest floor. Invading earthworms can eat away this entire layer, leaving mostly bare soil behind, and some of the wildflowers and young trees that grew in it then die. These facts suggest that earthworms ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: should be removed from gardens and farm fields.
can help the soil in some places but harm plants in others.
help forest plants grow by mixing fallen leaves into the soil.
lived in the Great Lakes region long before people arrived there.
items.explanation: In gardens and on farms, earthworms improve the soil. In Great Lakes forests, they eat the leaf layer that plants grow in, and some plants die. So earthworms help in some places and harm in others, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says gardeners and farmers welcome earthworms because they improve the soil, so it gives no reason to remove them there.

C.why_wrong: In these forests the worms eat the leaf layer the plants grow in, and some plants die.

D.why_wrong: The text says these forests had no earthworms until people brought them in.

sources.what: Great Lakes earthworm research (Cindy Hale): what earthworms do in agricultural systems we like, what they do in native hardwood forests we don't; they eliminate the duff layer, the rooting zone of forest plants, causing plant mortality; the region has no native earthworms

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology). Easy S7: two settings, opposite effects.

fixes: removed 'from Europe and Asia' and 'within just a few years' (not on the cited page); bait clause and plant loss reworded to the page
